result.summary: Hesiod finishes the account of Typhoeus' winds, then tells how Zeus is made king and takes wives, swallowing Metis and fathering gods and goddesses. The section lists the children of Zeus and the marriages of gods and heroes, and ends by turning to goddesses who bore children to mortals.

scenes.title: Winds from Typhoeus
scenes.summary: The harmful winds descend from Typhoeus, unlike the blessed Notus, Boreas and Zephyr. They wreck ships and ruin fields.
scenes.stakes: Sailors and farmers face ruin from the destructive winds.

scenes.title: Zeus reigns and swallows Metis
scenes.summary: The gods urge Zeus to rule and he distributes honours. He weds Metis and swallows her on the advice of Earth and Heaven to prevent a rival king.
scenes.stakes: Zeus risks being supplanted by a son wiser and stronger than he.

scenes.title: The wives and children of Zeus
scenes.summary: Zeus marries Themis, Eurynome, Demeter, Mnemosyne, Leto and Hera, who bear Hours, Fates, Graces, Persephone, Muses, Apollo, Artemis and others. Zeus bears Athene from his head and Hera bears Hephaestus alone.

scenes.title: Metis swallowed; Athena born
scenes.summary: Variant lines retell Hera's quarrel and Hephaestus' birth. Zeus swallows Metis and gives birth to Athena by the river Trito.
scenes.stakes: Zeus fears a child stronger than his thunderbolt.

scenes.title: Other divine and heroic marriages
scenes.summary: Children are born to Amphitrite, Aphrodite, Maia, Semele, Alcmena and Perseis. Hephaestus, Dionysus and Heracles marry, and Heracles joins the gods.

scenes.title: Farewell and invocation
scenes.summary: The poet bids farewell to the gods and lands and asks the Muses to sing of goddesses who lay with mortals.

alias_notes.explanation: Epithet of Athene, linked to the river Trito.
Epithet of Aphrodite, named from the island Cythera; the text also says golden Aphrodite.
Another name for the god of the underworld.

notable_quotes.reason: Marks Dionysus as a mortal woman's immortal son.
Zeus swallows Metis, a key succession-myth moment.

analysis.text: After the victory over the Titans, Zeus secures his rule by swallowing Metis, preventing any successor and absorbing wisdom.
The catalogue of marriages shows an ordered cosmos, with gods embodying justice, fate, song and war.

legacy.text: The birth of Athena from Zeus' head became a major subject of Greek art, as on the Parthenon's east pediment.

fun_facts.text: Lines 929a-929t are bracketed in this translation as a variant passage, and a lacuna interrupts the text.

language_notes.text: Typhoeus is the monstrous son of Earth whom Zeus defeated just before this passage; the harmful winds are his offspring.
The Titans were the older generation of gods, whom the Olympians defeated in a long war before choosing Zeus as king.
Athene is the goddess of wisdom and war; the Greek-style epithet 'bright-eyed' (glaukopis) is often rendered 'grey-eyed' as well.
Tritogeneia is an epithet of Athene; its meaning is uncertain, perhaps 'Triton-born' or 'born of the head'.
Horae are the Hours or Seasons; the translator adds the Greek names with English meanings in brackets.
Aidoneus is Hades, lord of the dead, who carried Persephone to the underworld; Zeus allowed the abduction.
The aegis is a divine shield or goatskin cloak associated with Zeus, symbolising his power to terrify.
The fair-cheeked daughter of Ocean and Tethys is Metis; her name means 'Thought' or 'Counsel', as the text notes. The lacuna marks a gap in the manuscripts.
'Aether' is the bright upper air, the sky region where Zeus dwells.
Pallas is a frequent title attached to Athene; its origin is uncertain.
Earth-Shaker is an epithet of Poseidon, god of the sea and earthquakes; he is not named here.
Cytherea is a name for Aphrodite, linked to the island of Cythera.
'Buxom' here is an old sense meaning obliging or gracious, not its modern sense.
The farewell to gods and lands is a conventional hymn ending, here closing the poem's divine genealogies.

context_notes.text: Metis means 'cunning intelligence'. She is a daughter of Ocean and Tethys, and Zeus's first wife.
Mnemosyne means 'Memory'. Her daughters, the Muses, inspire poets, which is why Hesiod invokes them.
Hephaestus is the lame smith god of the forge; here Hera bears him alone in anger at Zeus's birth of Athene.
Zeus swallows Metis because it was prophesied that her child would be stronger than its father; Athena's birth from his head averts this.
Semele was a mortal princess of Thebes. Her son Dionysus became a god, as the poet says.
Heracles' toils were the labours he performed; afterwards he was received among the gods and married Hebe, goddess of youth.
Medea, born here, is later known in the Argonaut story as the helper of Jason and a sorceress.

literary_notes.text: The winds 'rush' and are 'raging', with 'evil' blasts, as if they were hostile creatures with intent to harm.
Zeus's trick and swallowing of Metis anticipate Athene's later birth from his head.
The prophecy of a son who would overthrow Zeus shows the cycle of succession, a theme throughout the poem.
A string of titles for Athene ('the awful, the strife-stirring, the host-leader') builds her formidable character.
Metis, whose name means Thought, is deceived by Zeus, though she is very wise.
The contrast 'a mortal woman an immortal son' sets mortal and immortal side by side in compact form.
The poet's exclamation 'Happy he!' breaks from narration into direct praise of Heracles' reward.
The poet turns again to the Muses, as at the poem's opening, and sets up the next poem's theme of goddesses and mortals.
